blocks.text: So far this module has assumed one instance fails and another one takes over.
Disaster recovery is about something bigger, a whole region going dark or a database getting corrupted.
It means having a plan you already wrote down, not one you invent while everything is on fire.
1. Disaster Recovery Is Not the Same as Self Healing

blocks.alt: Self healing handles small failures while disaster recovery handles major ones

blocks.text: Restarting a crashed process is routine. Kubernetes or your process manager already does that for you.
Disaster recovery covers the case where the entire environment your server runs in is gone.
That could be a region outage, a corrupted database, or an account level security incident.
The tools are different too. You are restoring from backups, not just starting a new container.
2. What Could Actually Go Wrong
A cloud region can lose power, networking, or simply become unreachable for hours.
A database can be corrupted by a bad migration, a bug, or an attacker, not just accidentally deleted.
Credentials can leak, forcing you to rotate everything and rebuild trust from a clean slate.

items: A cloud region or availability zone goes offline for an extended period.
A database is corrupted by a bad deploy, a runaway script, or a hostile actor.
A cloud account is locked, suspended, or compromised.
A dependency your MCP server relies on disappears or changes its API without warning.

blocks.text: 3. List Everything Your Server Depends On
Before planning recovery, write down every piece of state your MCP server cannot function without.
Most teams are surprised how much of this lives outside version control, hiding in a dashboard somewhere.

blocks.text: 4. Backing Up the Database

blocks.alt: A live database is backed up on a regular schedule

blocks.text: The database is usually the most important thing to protect, and the easiest to get wrong.
A nightly logical dump, shipped somewhere other than the same disk, is the minimum bar.

code.content:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -euo pipefail
TIMESTAMP=$(date -u +%Y%m%dT%H%M%SZ)
FILE="mcp-db-${TIMESTAMP}.sql.gz"

pg_dump "$DATABASE_URL" | gzip > "/tmp/${FILE}"

aws s3 cp "/tmp/${FILE}" "s3://mcp-backups-offsite/db/${FILE}" \
  --sse AES256

echo "backup written to s3://mcp-backups-offsite/db/${FILE}"

blocks.text: The offsite bucket should sit in a different region and a different account than the database itself.
5. Backing Up Configuration and Secrets
Configuration and secrets are easy to forget because they rarely change, until the day you need them.
Export them from your secrets manager on a schedule, encrypted, and store that export separately too.

code.content:
aws secretsmanager list-secrets --query "SecretList[].Name" --output text \
  | tr '\t' '\n' \
  | while read -r name; do
      aws secretsmanager get-secret-value --secret-id "$name" \
        --query SecretString --output text \
        >> /tmp/secrets-export.jsonl
    done

gpg --symmetric --cipher-algo AES256 /tmp/secrets-export.jsonl

blocks.title: Never store secret exports unencrypted
blocks.content: A plaintext secrets dump sitting in a bucket is a bigger risk than the disaster you were preparing for.

blocks.text: 6. Recovery Point Objective, How Much Data You Can Lose

blocks.alt: Recovery point objective is compared against recovery time objective

blocks.text: Recovery point objective is the maximum amount of data you are willing to lose if disaster strikes.
A nightly backup means an RPO of roughly one day, whatever changed since the last dump is gone.
If that is too much, you need more frequent backups or continuous replication, not just a better script.
7. Recovery Time Objective, How Long Recovery Can Take
Recovery time objective is how long you can be down before it becomes unacceptable to your users.
An RTO of thirty minutes and an RTO of two days call for very different levels of automation.

blocks.text: 8. Writing the Recovery Plan Down
A recovery plan that exists only in one engineer’s head is not a plan, it is a single point of failure.
During an actual incident, people are stressed, tired, and thinking less clearly than usual.
A written runbook gives whoever is on call something concrete to follow instead of improvising.

items: What counts as a disaster, and who has the authority to declare one.
Exact commands to restore the database, in order, with no steps assumed.
Where secrets and access credentials for the recovery process itself are stored.
Who to notify, and what to tell users while recovery is in progress.

blocks.text: 9. Designing for a Region Going Down

blocks.alt: A primary region failing over to a standby region using offsite backups

blocks.text: The most demanding disaster scenario is losing an entire cloud region, not just one server.
Recovering from that means your backups, and ideally a standby environment, must live outside that region.
A standby environment does not need to run at full scale, it just needs to exist and be ready to scale up.
10. Restoring a Corrupted Database Step by Step

blocks.alt: A corrupted database is restored from the last good backup step by step

blocks.text: Corruption is trickier than total loss, because the bad data can look valid at first glance.
The safe move is to restore into a fresh database, verify it, then cut traffic over.

code.content:
# 1. Create a fresh database, never restore over the live one directly
createdb mcp_restore_check

# 2. Pull the most recent known good backup from offsite storage
aws s3 cp s3://mcp-backups-offsite/db/mcp-db-20260630T020000Z.sql.gz /tmp/

# 3. Restore into the fresh database
gunzip -c /tmp/mcp-db-20260630T020000Z.sql.gz | psql mcp_restore_check

# 4. Run sanity checks before pointing the server at it
psql mcp_restore_check -c "select count(*) from tool_calls;"

# 5. Only after checks pass, repoint the server's DATABASE_URL

blocks.text: 11. Automating Backup Verification
A backup you have never restored is a guess, not a backup.
A simple job that restores the latest backup into a throwaway database catches broken backups early.

code.content:
# runs nightly, right after the backup job
LATEST=$(aws s3 ls s3://mcp-backups-offsite/db/ | sort | tail -n 1 | awk '{print $4}')
aws s3 cp "s3://mcp-backups-offsite/db/${LATEST}" /tmp/verify.sql.gz
createdb mcp_backup_verify --if-not-exists
gunzip -c /tmp/verify.sql.gz | psql mcp_backup_verify
psql mcp_backup_verify -c "select count(*) from tool_calls;" || exit 1
dropdb mcp_backup_verify

blocks.text: If this job ever fails, treat it as urgently as a real outage. Your safety net just tore.
12. Testing the Plan on Purpose

blocks.alt: A recovery plan is tested on purpose rather than only during a real incident

blocks.text: A disaster recovery plan you have never rehearsed usually turns out to be wrong in some small but painful way.
Schedule a drill, pick a scenario, and actually restore into a test environment following the written runbook.
Time the whole exercise and compare it against your stated recovery time objective.

blocks.title: Drills find the gaps improvisation hides
blocks.content: A missing permission, a stale credential, or an outdated command only shows up when you actually try the steps.

blocks.text: 13. Who Does What During an Incident

blocks.alt: Each role has a clear responsibility during an incident response

blocks.text: When something big breaks, unclear ownership wastes the first, most valuable minutes.
Assign roles ahead of time so nobody is debating who is in charge while data is still at risk.

items: Incident lead, decides when to declare a disaster and when it is resolved.
Executor, runs the actual restore commands from the runbook.
Communicator, updates users and stakeholders on status.
Scribe, records a timeline of what happened for the review afterward.

blocks.text: 14. Common Ways the Plan Itself Goes Stale
A recovery plan is a living document, and living documents rot if nobody tends to them.
Credentials referenced in the runbook expire, servers get renamed, and commands quietly stop matching reality.
Tie a review of the plan to any major infrastructure change, not just to a calendar reminder.
15. Keeping Backups and Plans Current Together
Backups and the plan to use them need to evolve together, or the plan quietly stops matching reality.
When you add a new datastore to your MCP server, add it to the backup script and the runbook the same day.
Treat the runbook as part of the system, reviewed in the same pull requests as the infrastructure it describes.
Worked Example: A Small Team’s Disaster Recovery Setup
A small team running one MCP server sets an RPO of one day and an RTO of four hours.
They run the nightly database backup script, ship it to an offsite bucket in a second region.
A backup verification job restores that dump into a scratch database every morning and checks row counts.

code.content:
# quarterly drill, run against a disposable environment
./scripts/restore-latest-backup.sh --target disaster-drill-env
./scripts/smoke-test.sh --env disaster-drill-env
echo "recovery completed in: $SECONDS seconds"

blocks.text: The written runbook lists exact commands, who is on call, and how to notify users, so nobody improvises.
Common Mistakes

items: Backing up the database but never testing whether the backup actually restores.
Storing backups in the same account or region as the primary system they protect.
Keeping the recovery plan only in one person’s memory instead of a shared document.
Never rehearsing the plan, so the first real test happens during an actual outage.
Forgetting configuration and secrets, and backing up only the database.

blocks.text: Practice
Write down every piece of state your own MCP server depends on, then check which parts are actually backed up.
Pick the riskiest gap, write a backup script for it, and schedule a verification job right alongside it.
Then run a small drill, restore that backup somewhere disposable, and time how long it takes.
Key Takeaway
Disaster recovery means planning for a whole region or database being gone, not just one process crashing.
Back up everything your server depends on, write the recovery steps down, and rehearse them before a real disaster forces you to.
